Ce dimanche, Montréal se parera des tein: This Sunday, Montréal will be dressed in the shimmering colours of the rainbow. The streets will echo with powerful music, and costumes will compete in creativity. The Pride parade will be in full swing. But behind this festive scene lie forgotten stories and experiences too often pushed into the shadows. Adam Darko's is one of them. We met this new Canadian of Algerian origin in Montréal, on the banks of the St. Lawrence River, to hear his story.
Adam Darko étend précautionneusement sa: Adam Darko carefully spreads his emerald-green picnic blanket on the ground. He picks a peaceful spot between a bush and a majestic tree. His gaze settles on the two imposing residential buildings that, like sentinels, flank either side of the stretch of urban beach where we are sitting.
Pour Adam, les contraintes liées au sexe: For Adam, the constraints tied to the sex he was assigned at birth and the barriers of his gender became apparent from a very young age. He knows that, like a stream, the incessant fluctuations between these two shores, the fluidity of the elements – sexuality, gender identity – follow their course, carving a path between pre-established contours.
Cette nouvelle a chamboulé la famille d’: The news shook Adam's family. Apart from one of his four brothers, everyone denounced and rejected him. “My father couldn't believe his ears and even threatened to kill me. My mother tried to protect me, but she couldn't openly stand by me. I felt incredibly alone within my circle of loved ones, especially since I also lost many friends.”
Avec le temps, Adam réussit à apaiser le: Over time, Adam managed to ease the tension with his father. With his brother's support, he convinced his mother that the threat hanging over him in Algeria was too great. “I remember coming home and telling my mother that I had been harassed again, that living there had become unbearable. Going outside had become dangerous. Little by little, she started to understand the situation.”
C’est donc par une belle journée ensolei: And so, on a beautiful sunny day in August 2017, the young Algerian left his homeland for Malaysia. Once there, he shared daily life with the friend who had recommended he go into exile in that country. After a few months, he found housing and a job under the table, since he had no work permit.
« Une fois installé, j’ai entamé ma tran: “Once I was settled, I began my physical transition. I bought hormones on the black market. Given my vulnerability as a migrant, the seller practically swindled me, selling me the hormones at an exorbitant price and giving me inadequate instructions. The hormones I was taking were supposed to be used over a longer period and not as frequently as he had told me,” he says.
Les souvenirs remontent et engourdissent: The memories come flooding back and numb Adam. His eyes, framed by long black lashes, close, and his head tilts toward the sky as the leaves of the trees swirl in the breeze. He brushes his beard before continuing: “It was really risky, injecting myself with hormones without any reliable references. I relied on my friends' advice, but their expertise wasn't necessarily better than mine. I don't recommend that approach. But at the time, as a tourist, I had no other option.”
Malgré cette prise de risque, Adam dit a: Despite the risks he took, Adam says he lived a relatively pleasant life in Malaysia. But the lack of a stable immigration status weighed on him. “I only had a tourist visa, and it constantly plunged me into anxiety. My life was one perpetual worry. I tried to get a student visa, but it was refused. I also saw several of my friends spend considerable sums on processing immigration files and deal with lawyers who ended up pocketing the money without even filing the applications.”
Pendant ce temps, Adam est en contact su: Meanwhile, Adam was in contact online with the Arab LGBTQ+ community, who suggested he claim asylum in Malaysia. However, <l1>refugees have no legal status there; the authorities make no distinction between undocumented migrants and refugees.</l1> Refugees have no right to protection. They are liable to be turned back and live in constant fear of being arrested and expelled from the country.
Adam sollicite tout de même le statut de: Adam applied for refugee status with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Kuala Lumpur anyway. He hoped to benefit from the protection of the international organization. The process involves in-depth interviews and a long wait for possible resettlement in another country. In the meantime, however, no protection is offered.
Pour prolonger son visa de tourisme en M: To extend his tourist visa in Malaysia, Adam had to leave the country and go to Indonesia. But on his return to Malaysia, as he came back for an interview with a UNHCR officer, he ran into a major obstacle: border agents noticed that his ID photo did not match his physical appearance. Discovering that he was transgender and that he had illegally extended his visa, they denied him entry into Malaysia. Despite his refugee claim document, he was held at the airport, without his belongings or passport, and spent the night there.
Le processus d’entretien de réinstallati: The UNHCR resettlement interview process went ahead, but Adam was expelled to Indonesia the day after his return to Malaysia. In Indonesia, he was refused entry again, because Malaysia had not authorized him to pass through. Once more, his refugee claim file offered him no protection. The Indonesian authorities even considered sending him back to Algeria, an option that was out of the question.
Son récit nous glace ; Adam nous offre u: His story chills us; Adam offers us a reprieve. He picks up a speaker he brought with him to the beach, and the voice of Algerian singer Naïma D'ziria rings out: “O lovely goldfinch with yellow wings, red cheeks, and dark eyes. For years you have been in a sad cage. Singing in a soft, wistful voice, no one knows where your song comes from.”* Adam follows with his eyes a little bird that disappears into the trees. A smile forms on his lips, then his face darkens, his gaze fixed on the reflections of the sun in the windows facing us.
« Les premiers jours passés dans cet aér: “The first days I spent in that Jakarta airport, I felt like I was in a cage. My passport was a source of deep humiliation. I was degraded and treated like a criminal,” he confides.
Les jours s’écoulent alors lentement, ju: The days then dragged on, until a UNHCR officer contacted Adam. “He told me they were in talks with Canada and thought the country might be interested in my case.” A smile pulls at the corners of his lips. “When I lived in Algiers, I followed the Pride celebrations in Montréal. The idea that Canada might one day welcome me was an immense hope for me. Canada became my anchor, my lifeline. It's the only thing that kept me afloat during those 20 nights spent on the airport floor.”
Après trois semaines infernales, l’appel: After three hellish weeks, the long-awaited call came: Adam could leave this limbo and fly to Canada the very next day. On his last night in Indonesia, lying on the airport floor, he let himself be carried away by his dreams, thinking about his new life. “A euphoria I had never felt before washed over me. As if my whole being were floating on a cloud, suspended. An almost unreal feeling, like a dream coming to life. It took me a while to realize that all of this was real. Everything seemed almost too good to be true.”
Aujourd’hui Canadien, Adam trouve que le: Now a Canadian, Adam finds that the charm of his first Pride parade has lost some of its force. “The parade has become an opportunity for companies and brands to promote themselves. It has become a show of supposed support for 2SLGBTQ+ people, but one that doesn't translate into real investment in our lives, our power and our aspirations,” he says.
Il demeure toutefois convaincu que cette: He remains convinced, however, that the parade still holds significant political meaning. “By taking part, you assert your presence and claim your right to exist. It has a special meaning for those who haven't had, or don't currently have, the privilege of being themselves in complete safety and freedom,” he explains.
Il évoque aussi une autre déception, cel: He also mentions another disappointment, this one tied to the Gay Village. “I remember that at first, I was very happy to hang out in that neighbourhood. But over time, I began to notice microaggressions,” he says, shaking his head. “You get the feeling that you're not really part of the group, that you're not represented. Unless you're a gay, cisgender and generally white man, it can be hard to find your place in the Village. There aren't even any lesbian or trans bars. If you look closely, most of the activities there are centred on the gay community.”
Le jeune Adam poursuit : « Ne se souvien: Adam continues: “Don't they remember who started all this? Who threw the first bricks at Stonewall? It was trans women of colour, and yet they can't find their place in this rainbow village.”
Puis, il déclare avec optimisme : « Nous: Then he declares with optimism: “We still have a long way to go, but at least we're on the right track.”
<strong>Le privilège de passer inaperçu: The privilege of going unnoticed: a double-edged sword
Après son arrivée au Canada, Adam a cont: After arriving in Canada, Adam continued his hormonal transition and had a mastectomy, a procedure to remove the breasts to achieve a more masculine chest. This transformation allows him to “pass” as a cisgender, heterosexual man. Unless you know him personally, you can't guess that he's trans. “Generally, it's a privilege, because I'm invisible and I don't attract the attention of intolerant or hateful people.”
C’est, selon lui, ce qui lui permet de s: This, he says, is what allows him to go into Maghrebi neighbourhoods without risking verbal abuse. “I'd even say that in those settings, I feel safer and more confident than women do,” he says, referring to cafés, which are generally frequented by men. “I don't reveal my transgender identity or my sexual orientation; I keep a low profile to avoid any conflict.”
Il souligne cependant que la communauté: He points out, however, that the Maghrebi community is not homogeneous, and that not all of its members are transphobic: “There's a lot of fear on our side (2SLGBTQ+). A deep-rooted fear that comes from the discrimination we faced from our own compatriots, in our countries. Sometimes that fear settles in us and can lead us to judge others indiscriminately.”
Adam laisse échapper un soupir. « Enfin,: Adam lets out a sigh. “Finally, I'm home,” he says. As he speaks to us, a mother duck and her ducklings pass near us. The scene reminds him of his own family: “I've only seen my mother on a screen since 2017.” Now that he holds a Canadian passport, he glimpses the possibility of reuniting with her outside Algeria.
Le ciel s’assombrit, Adam s’apprête à re: The sky darkens, and Adam prepares to head home. We leave him with the impression that, like the discreet oases of the Algerian Sahara, he has always been this river that dances without end. His flows are an enigma hidden in historical accounts, a presence concealed beneath grains of sand – and yet the water persists. So it is that Adam never faltered. Like the stream that flows relentlessly, he has migrated toward the essence of his being.

Si ce Montréalais se présente aujourd’hu: While this Montrealer now identifies as a queer transgender man, that wasn’t the case when he was growing up in Algiers. Back then, he saw himself differently. “Toward the end of my teens, when I was still in Algeria, I was seeing a young woman and I called myself a lesbian,” he says, laughing. In fact, the sex he was assigned at birth, female, didn’t match his true identity. “After I opened up to my girlfriend at the time about how I felt about my body and my gender, she asked me, ‘Are you trans?’ At that point, I didn’t really get what the word meant. But as I did more research, that identity resonated with me,” the 27-year-old recalls with a faint smile.
Après cette révélation, Adam envisage de: After this revelation, Adam begins thinking about leaving Algeria, the country where he was born. “I kept telling my father we needed to get passports, even though we had no trips planned.” As he approaches 20, he reaches a breaking point. “I felt like I was about to explode. And then one day, it all came pouring out. I couldn’t take the pressure of having to conform to gender expectations anymore. I spontaneously came out to my family as a trans man.”
Il se tait, tandis qu’un groupe de jeune: He falls silent as a group of young people walks by. A few seconds pass, and his brown eyes settle on the gap between two buildings. Then he picks up again, his tone calm: “After I came out, I cut my hair really short and started wearing more traditionally masculine clothes.”
Cette décision témoigne d’un grand coura: It was a decision that took great courage, because in Algeria, queerness is not socially accepted. Adam’s sudden change in appearance and his more androgynous style did not go unnoticed, and they exposed him to constant harassment on the street. On top of that, the Algerian Penal Code punishes homosexuality and “outrage to public decency” with sentences of up to three years in prison.
Perdu, Adam entre en contact avec la com: Feeling lost, Adam reaches out to Algeria’s queer community. With no support, he decides to start a YouTube channel to share his experience. “Lots of queer Algerians and North Africans, and people from Western countries, started getting in touch with me.” That community turned out to be vital for Adam; it gave him support, kinship and solutions. “I met a lot of Algerians who were also thinking about leaving the country for safety reasons. Everyone had their own story and their own ways of getting out. One of my online friends chose Malaysia and really recommended it to me, because it’s one of the countries where Algerians don’t need to apply for an entry visa.”
L’année suivant son <em>coming out</em>,: The year after his coming out, Adam convinces his parents to let him go study in Malaysia. “The truth is, I didn’t have a clear plan, but leaving Algeria was already a better option than staying. So I came up with a lie: I said I wanted to continue my studies in Malaysia. Even though they hesitated right up until the last minute, the fact that it’s a Muslim country worked in my favour.”
En 2018, Adam quitte enfin sa cage pour: In 2018, Adam finally leaves his cage and lands in Montréal, where he unpacks his bags and settles down. That first summer, he finally fulfills his wish to attend the Pride parade. “I remember going with some queer Algerian friends I’d met online. During the march, I saw someone carrying the Algerian flag. That touched me deeply. I felt validated. In fact, in 2019, I carried the flag of my home country myself. I was truly proud.”
Selon lui, il existe beaucoup de racisme: According to him, there is a lot of racism in queer spaces, where white people are the vast majority. “People don’t understand where we come from. They can be queer, but that doesn’t stop them from being intolerant toward us. They always think we get around on camels back home, as if there were no civilization in our countries of origin,” the new Canadian laments. He remembers that at a party in the Gay Village, he was refused something as simple as playing music from his country or from the Arab-Amazigh world. “It’s exhausting because we constantly have to educate them. Explain to them that queer identity isn’t a Western invention. There were queer figures before and after Islam; just think of poets like Aboû Nouwâs or actors like Hanan El Tawil, who is a trans woman. [Gender normativity] is really a colonial concept that we’ve unfortunately internalized,” he adds.
Le soleil commence à décliner dans le ci: The sun begins to sink in the city sky, tinting the St. Lawrence with an orange glow. Adam runs his hand over his beard and continues: “These perceptions are really problematic, because when queer and trans people see me, they don’t think I’m part of their community. Sometimes I get associated with the image of bearded Arab men that the media has often portrayed as terrorists or as a source of intolerance and hate.”
Selon Adam, il existe un grand fossé dan: According to Adam, there is a wide gap in the North African community between straight and queer people. “At the Pride parade, I rarely see straight Maghrebi people who are allies and who support us. It makes me sad, even though I understand the reasons**. I would have liked for us to mix, safely,” he confides.
